# Systems of linear equations {#sec-linear-systems}

[Core]{.level-badge .core}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## In this chapter you will

- write a system of linear equations as $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ and as an augmented matrix
- picture a system in two ways: as lines or planes that meet (the row picture), and as a combination of columns (the column picture)
- explain why a system has exactly one solution, no solution or infinitely many, and never anything in between
- recognise homogeneous systems, and how their solutions describe all the solutions of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$
:::

**Builds on** @sec-multiplication, @sec-determinants, @sec-inverses.

Part I treated a matrix as a table, and as a machine that moves points. Part II turns to the question that matrices are most often used to answer: **given $\M{A}$ and $\vect{b}$, find every $\vect{x}$ with $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$**. Structures, circuits, chemical plants, data fits and computer simulations all come down to it, often with thousands or millions of unknowns.

This chapter sets up the problem and asks what the answer can look like. @sec-gaussian-elimination gives the method for finding it.

## Build intuition

The app draws each equation of a system as a line (with two unknowns) or a plane (with three). A solution is a point that lies on all of them at once. This is the **row picture**. The app also has a second view, the **column picture**; leave that for now, as it comes back later in the chapter, once it has been explained.

Things to try:

- With two unknowns, try the three presets. How do the lines sit when there is one solution, none and infinitely many?
- Change one number at a time in **One solution** until the lines become parallel. Which numbers did you change, and how is the new pair of equations related?
- Switch to three unknowns and try each preset, turning the picture to see how the planes sit. There are several different ways for three planes to have no common point.

## The ideas

### From equations to matrices

A **linear equation** in the unknowns $x_1, \dots, x_n$ is one in which each unknown is only multiplied by a number, and the results are added: $3x_1 - 2x_2 + x_3 = 4$ is linear, but $x_1x_2 = 4$ and $\sin x_1 = 0$ are not. A **system** of linear equations is several of these that must all hold at once.

Every system can be written as one matrix equation. For example,
$$
\begin{aligned}
2x + y - z &= 8 \\
-3x - y + 2z &= -11 \\
-2x + y + 2z &= -3
\end{aligned}
$$
is $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ with
$$
\M{A} = \mat{2 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2},
$$
$$
\vect{x} = \mat{x \\ y \\ z},
$$
$$
\vect{b} = \mat{8 \\ -11 \\ -3}.
$$
Each row of $\M{A}$ holds the coefficients of one equation, each column belongs to one unknown, and $\vect{b}$ holds the right-hand sides. Multiplying out $\M{A}\vect{x}$ by the row-times-column rule (@sec-multiplication) gives back the left-hand sides.

Since the unknowns are only labels for the columns, the whole system can be stored as the **augmented matrix** $[\M{A} \mid \vect{b}]$: the coefficients with the right-hand sides attached as an extra column.
$$
\amat{rrr|r}{2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\ -3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -3}
$$
The vertical line stands for the equals signs. This is the form that @sec-gaussian-elimination works with.

A **solution** is a vector $\vect{x}$ that makes every equation true. Solving the system means finding all of them. This one has exactly one, $\vect{x} = (2, 3, -1)\T$, which you can check by substituting.

::: {#ex-linear-systems-1 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 1: setting up a system

A workshop melts down three scrap alloys to make a new one. By mass, alloy 1 is 60% copper, 30% zinc and 10% tin; alloy 2 is 80% copper, 10% zinc and 10% tin; and alloy 3 is 50% copper, 20% zinc and 30% tin. How much of each is needed to make 100 kg containing 60 kg of copper, 22 kg of zinc and 18 kg of tin? Write the problem as a matrix equation, in the row picture and the column picture.

**Solution.** Let $x_1$, $x_2$ and $x_3$ be the masses of the three alloys in kilograms. Counting each metal gives one equation, for copper, zinc and tin in turn:
$$
\begin{aligned}
0.6x_1 + 0.8x_2 + 0.5x_3 &= 60 \\
0.3x_1 + 0.1x_2 + 0.2x_3 &= 22 \\
0.1x_1 + 0.1x_2 + 0.3x_3 &= 18
\end{aligned}
$$
So $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ with
$$
\M{A} = \mat{0.6 & 0.8 & 0.5 \\ 0.3 & 0.1 & 0.2 \\ 0.1 & 0.1 & 0.3},
$$
$$
\vect{b} = \mat{60 \\ 22 \\ 18}.
$$
In the row picture, each metal gives a plane, and the answer is the point where the three planes meet. In the column picture, each column of $\M{A}$ is the make-up of one alloy, and the question is how much of each alloy to mix to get the make-up $\vect{b}$:
$$
x_1\mat{0.6 \\ 0.3 \\ 0.1} + x_2\mat{0.8 \\ 0.1 \\ 0.1} + x_3\mat{0.5 \\ 0.2 \\ 0.3} = \mat{60 \\ 22 \\ 18}.
$$
The solution, found by the methods of the next chapter or in code below, is $x_1 = 40$, $x_2 = 20$, $x_3 = 40$. Check the copper: $0.6 \times 40 + 0.8 \times 20 + 0.5 \times 40 = 60$ ✓. (There was no need for a fourth equation saying the total is 100 kg: each column adds up to 1, so the three metals automatically total $x_1 + x_2 + x_3$.)
:::

### The row picture

Read the system one equation, that is one row, at a time.

- **Two unknowns.** Each equation $ax + by = c$ is a straight line in the plane. A solution is a point on every line: where the lines cross.
- **Three unknowns.** Each equation $ax + by + cz = d$ is a flat **plane** in space. A solution is a point on every plane.

Two lines in a plane normally cross at one point, but they may be parallel, or be the same line. Three planes in space normally meet at one point, but there are more ways for this to fail, as the app shows. Two of the planes may be parallel. Or each pair may meet in a line with the three lines parallel, forming a long triangular tube with nothing inside it common to all three.

### The column picture

Now read the system one column at a time. Start with the two equations of the app's first example,
$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + 2y &= 7 \\
4x - 5y &= -6.
\end{aligned}
$$
Two vectors are equal exactly when their entries are equal, one by one. So the pair of equations says the same thing as a single equation between vectors, with the first equation in the top entries and the second in the bottom ones:
$$
\mat{3x + 2y \\ 4x - 5y} = \mat{7 \\ -6}.
$$
Split the left-hand side into the part with $x$ and the part with $y$, and take each unknown outside its vector:
$$
\mat{3x \\ 4x} + \mat{2y \\ -5y} = \mat{7 \\ -6},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
x\mat{3 \\ 4} + y\mat{2 \\ -5} = \mat{7 \\ -6}.
$$
Nothing has been added or lost; the same six numbers have only been rearranged.

- **Reading down** gives the columns of $\M{A}$. The first vector, $\vect{a}_1 = (3, 4)\T$, holds the coefficients of $x$: 3 from the first equation and 4 from the second. The second, $\vect{a}_2 = (2, -5)\T$, holds the coefficients of $y$. The right-hand side $\vect{b} = (7, -6)\T$ holds the right-hand sides.
- **Reading across** gives the equations back. The top entries say $3x + 2y = 7$, and the bottom entries say $4x - 5y = -6$.

The question has changed its form. Instead of "which point lies on both lines?", it asks **how much of $\vect{a}_1$ and how much of $\vect{a}_2$ make $\vect{b}$?** The answer is $x = 1$ and $y = 2$: one of the first column and two of the second,
$$
1\mat{3 \\ 4} + 2\mat{2 \\ -5} = \mat{3 \\ 4} + \mat{4 \\ -10} = \mat{7 \\ -6}.
$$
@fig-two-pictures shows both pictures of this system. In the row picture, the solution is the point $(1, 2)$ where the lines cross. In the column picture, it is the recipe for reaching $\vect{b}$: go along $\vect{a}_1$ once, then along $\vect{a}_2$ twice.

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left, the row picture: the lines 3x + 2y = 7 and 4x − 5y = −6 cross at the point (1, 2). Right, the column picture: arrows a1 = (3, 4) and a2 = (2, −5) from the origin, and a path that goes along a1 once to (3, 4) and then along a2 twice to b = (7, −6)."
#| label: fig-two-pictures
#| fig-cap: "The same system in two pictures. Left: each equation is a line, and the solution is where they cross. Right: each column is an arrow, made from the coefficients of one unknown, and the solution says how much of each arrow to take to reach b: one of a₁ (blue, the coefficients of x), then two of a₂ (orange, the coefficients of y)."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code for this figure"
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blue, orange, green = "#2153b8", "#9c5208", "#0a7050"
a1, a2, b = np.array([3, 4]), np.array([2, -5]), np.array([7, -6])
x, y = 1, 2

fig, (L, R) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.6))

# Row picture: one line per equation
t = np.linspace(-2, 4, 2)
# grey lines, so that blue and orange can mean "x" and "y" in the column picture
L.plot(t, (7 - 3 * t) / 2, color="0.25", lw=2.2, label="3x + 2y = 7")
L.plot(t, (4 * t + 6) / 5, color="0.45", lw=2.2, ls="--", label="4x − 5y = −6")
L.plot(x, y, "o", color=green, ms=8)
L.annotate("(1, 2)", (x, y), xytext=(10, -14), textcoords="offset points", color=green, fontweight="bold")
L.set_xlim(-2, 4); L.set_ylim(-2, 5)
L.set_title("Row picture: where do the lines cross?", fontsize=11)
L.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)

# Column picture: one arrow per column, then the path to b
def arrow(ax, p, q, colour, lw=2.2, alpha=1.0):
    ax.annotate("", xy=q, xytext=p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=colour, lw=lw,
                                                     alpha=alpha, mutation_scale=14, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))

O = np.zeros(2)
arrow(R, O, a2, orange, alpha=0.45)
R.annotate("a₂ = (2, −5)", a2, xytext=(8, -8), textcoords="offset points", color=orange)
arrow(R, O, x * a1, blue, lw=3)
R.annotate("a₁ = (3, 4)", a1, xytext=(6, 4), textcoords="offset points", color=blue)
arrow(R, x * a1, x * a1 + y * a2, orange, lw=3)
R.annotate("2a₂", x * a1 + 0.5 * y * a2, xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", color=orange)
R.plot(*b, "o", color=green, ms=8)
R.annotate("b = (7, −6)", b, xytext=(-40, -20), textcoords="offset points", color=green, fontweight="bold")
R.set_xlim(-2, 9); R.set_ylim(-8, 6)
R.set_title("Column picture: 1 a₁ + 2 a₂ = b", fontsize=11)

for ax in (L, R):
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8); ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The same rearrangement works for any system. By the column view of multiplication (@sec-multiplication), $\M{A}\vect{x}$ is a linear combination of the columns of $\M{A}$, so the three equations at the start of this section say
$$
x\mat{2 \\ -3 \\ -2} + y\mat{1 \\ -1 \\ 1} + z\mat{-1 \\ 2 \\ 2} = \mat{8 \\ -11 \\ -3}.
$$
Again, reading down each vector gives the coefficients of one unknown, and reading across the top entries gives back the first equation, $2x + y - z = 8$. Solving the system means finding **how much of each column to take** to make $\vect{b}$.

Here is the systems explorer again, now opened in the column picture. The coefficient boxes are coloured by column, and under the picture the vector equation is read across, row by row, to give back the equations.

Things to try:

- In **One solution**, find each of the six numbers of the equations in the picture. Which arrow is made from the coefficients of $x$, and which from those of $y$?
- Change the right-hand sides to $5$ and $-1$, leaving the coefficients alone. The arrows $\vect{a}_1$ and $\vect{a}_2$ don't move; only $\vect{b}$ does. How much of each arrow do you need now?
- Try **No solution** and **Infinitely many**. The two arrows lie along the same line. Which right-hand sides can they reach? Switch to the row picture to see the same thing as parallel lines.
- With three unknowns, turn the picture and follow the path along each column in turn to $\vect{b}$. This is exactly the question asked by the linear combination explorer in @sec-arithmetic, and the bakery's shopping list there was a column picture: the columns were recipes, the amounts were numbers of batches, and $\vect{b}$ was the total of each ingredient.

The two pictures describe the same system and always give the same answer. The row picture is easier to draw. The column picture is often easier to *reason* with, and it is the one that Parts III and IV build on.

### One solution, none or infinitely many

Every system of linear equations has **exactly one solution**, **no solution** or **infinitely many solutions**. It can never have exactly two, or exactly five.

The reason is linearity. Suppose $\vect{p}$ and $\vect{q}$ are two different solutions, so $\M{A}\vect{p} = \vect{b}$ and $\M{A}\vect{q} = \vect{b}$. Then for any number $t$,
$$
\M{A}\big(\vect{p} + t(\vect{q} - \vect{p})\big) = \M{A}\vect{p} + t(\M{A}\vect{q} - \M{A}\vect{p}) = \vect{b} + t(\vect{b} - \vect{b}) = \vect{b}.
$$
So every point on the line through $\vect{p}$ and $\vect{q}$ is a solution too. Once there are two solutions, there are infinitely many.

A system with no solution is called **inconsistent**; one with at least one solution is **consistent**.

For a **square** system, with as many equations as unknowns, Part I has already given the test (@sec-determinants, @sec-inverses):

- if $\det\M{A} \neq 0$, there is exactly one solution for every $\vect{b}$, namely $\vect{x} = \M{A}^{-1}\vect{b}$;
- if $\det\M{A} = 0$, there is either no solution or infinitely many, depending on $\vect{b}$.

In the row picture, $\det\M{A} = 0$ means the lines are parallel, or the planes fail to meet at a single point. In the column picture, it means the columns all lie along one line (in two dimensions) or in one plane (in three), so they can only make vectors $\vect{b}$ that lie there too. If $\vect{b}$ is on that line or plane, it can be made in infinitely many ways; if it is not, it cannot be made at all.

::: {#ex-linear-systems-2 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 2: three planes with no common point

Show that this system has no solution, and describe the planes.
$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 3 \\
x - y + z &= 1 \\
2x + 2z &= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

**Solution.** Adding the first two equations gives $2x + 2z = 4$. But the third equation says $2x + 2z = 5$. Both cannot hold, so there is no solution: the system is inconsistent.

No two of the planes are parallel (no equation's coefficients are a multiple of another's), so each pair of planes meets in a line. But the three lines never meet: they are parallel, and the planes form a triangular tube (@fig-three-planes, left). This is the [**Triangular tube**](../apps/linear-systems.html?preset=Triangular%20tube){target="_blank" aria-label="Triangular tube preset in the systems explorer (opens in a new tab)"} preset in the app.
:::

::: {#ex-linear-systems-3 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 3: three planes through a line

Change the last right-hand side of Example 2 from 5 to 4. Find all the solutions.

**Solution.** Now adding the first two equations gives $2x + 2z = 4$, which *is* the third equation. So the third equation adds no new information, and the system is really the first two equations. Subtracting the second from the first gives $2y = 2$, so $y = 1$, and then the first equation says $x + z = 2$.

Any value of $z$ works, with $x = 2 - z$. Writing $z = t$, the solutions are
$$
\vect{x} = \mat{2 - t \\ 1 \\ t} = \mat{2 \\ 1 \\ 0} + t\mat{-1 \\ 0 \\ 1}
$$
for every number $t$: a line of solutions, along which all three planes meet, like the pages of an open book (@fig-three-planes, right). This matches @eq-general-solution. The vector $(2, 1, 0)\T$ is a particular solution, and $t(-1, 0, 1)\T$ runs through every solution of the homogeneous system.

![The planes of Examples 2 and 3, viewed along the direction $(-1, 0, 1)$, which lies in all three planes, so that each plane appears as a line. Left: each pair of planes meets, but the three lines where they meet are parallel and form a triangular tube (shaded), so there is no solution. Right: all three planes share one line, which appears as a single point.](images/three-planes.png){#fig-three-planes fig-alt="Two panels, each showing three planes edge on, as lines. Left, Example 2: the lines for x plus y plus z equals 3, x minus y plus z equals 1, and 2x plus 2z equals 5 form a small shaded triangle, with no point on all three. Right, Example 3: the lines for x plus y plus z equals 3, x minus y plus z equals 1, and 2x plus 2z equals 4 all pass through one point, labelled the line of solutions." width=90%}
:::

### Homogeneous systems

A system is **homogeneous** if every right-hand side is zero: $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$. It always has at least one solution, $\vect{x} = \zerovec$, called the **trivial solution**, so it can never be inconsistent. The only question is whether it has others. For a square matrix, it has non-trivial solutions exactly when $\det\M{A} = 0$. You have met this already: the invariant points of a transformation solve the homogeneous system $(\M{A} - \M{I})\vect{x} = \zerovec$ (@sec-invariant-lines).

Homogeneous systems describe the structure of every other system. If $\vect{p}$ is one solution of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ (a **particular solution**), then
$$
\text{every solution of } \M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b} \text{ is } \vect{p} + \vect{h}, \text{ where } \M{A}\vect{h} = \zerovec.
$$ {#eq-general-solution}
In words: the solutions of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ are the solutions of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$, shifted by $\vect{p}$. In the row picture, the solution set of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ is a point, line or plane, parallel to the one for $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$ through the origin. Exercise 5 asks you to prove it; @sec-gauss-jordan-rank uses it to write down every solution.

::: {#ex-linear-systems-4 .callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
### Example 4: balancing a chemical equation

When methane (natural gas, $\mathrm{CH_4}$) burns in oxygen ($\mathrm{O_2}$), it produces carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) and water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$). Find whole numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ to balance
$$
a\,\mathrm{CH_4} + b\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow c\,\mathrm{CO_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O}.
$$

**Solution.** A chemical reaction rearranges atoms but never creates or destroys them, so each element must appear equally often on both sides. Counting atoms of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen:
$$
\begin{aligned}
a &= c \quad\text{(carbon)} \\
4a &= 2d \quad\text{(hydrogen)} \\
2b &= 2c + d \quad\text{(oxygen)}
\end{aligned}
$$
Moving everything to the left gives a homogeneous system of three equations in four unknowns:
$$
\amat{rrrr|r}{1 & 0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2 & -1 & 0}.
$$
It has fewer equations than unknowns, so it has infinitely many solutions. That makes sense: if a set of numbers balances the equation, so does twice that set. Choose $a = 1$; then $c = 1$, $d = 2$, and $2b = 2 + 2$, so $b = 2$:
$$
\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}.
$$
:::

### More equations than unknowns, or fewer

Systems do not have to be square.

- **More equations than unknowns** (an **overdetermined** system), such as three lines in a plane: usually there is no solution, because three lines rarely pass through one point. This is the normal situation when fitting a model to measured data, and the fix is to look for the *best* approximate solution instead (@sec-orthogonality-least-squares).
- **Fewer equations than unknowns** (an **underdetermined** system), such as two planes in space: usually there are infinitely many solutions, because two planes that are not parallel meet in a whole line. There can still be none, if the planes are parallel.

## In code

Both languages solve square systems with one command, which uses the elimination method of @sec-gaussian-elimination. Always check the answer by multiplying back: the **residual** $\M{A}\vect{x} - \vect{b}$ should be zero, apart from tiny rounding errors.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[0.6, 0.8, 0.5],
              [0.3, 0.1, 0.2],
              [0.1, 0.1, 0.3]])
b = np.array([60, 22, 18])

x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)
print(A @ x - b)          # the residual: zero, up to rounding
```

When $\det\M{A} = 0$, `np.linalg.solve` stops with an error rather than guess:

```{python}
A2 = np.array([[1, 1, 1], [1, -1, 1], [2, 0, 2]])
b2 = np.array([3, 1, 5])
try:
    np.linalg.solve(A2, b2)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
    print("Error:", err)
```

To tell "no solution" from "infinitely many", compare the **rank** of $\M{A}$ with the rank of the augmented matrix. The rank counts the genuinely independent equations (@sec-gauss-jordan-rank explains it fully). If adding $\vect{b}$ increases the rank, $\vect{b}$ brings in an equation that contradicts the others, and there is no solution:

```{python}
Ab2 = np.column_stack([A2, b2])          # the augmented matrix [A | b]
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(A2), np.linalg.matrix_rank(Ab2))
```

## MATLAB

```matlab
A = [0.6 0.8 0.5;
     0.3 0.1 0.2;
     0.1 0.1 0.3];
b = [60; 22; 18];

x = A \ b
A*x - b              % the residual: zero, up to rounding
```

```{.text .code-output}
x =

    40
    20
    40

ans =

     0
     0
     0
```

Here the residual happens to be exactly zero. On another computer it might be something like `1.0e-14`: tiny, which is all that matters. When $\det\M{A} = 0$, MATLAB still returns an answer but warns that the matrix is singular, and the answer is meaningless (often `Inf` or `NaN`, "not a number"). Never ignore that warning.

To tell "no solution" from "infinitely many", compare the **rank** of $\M{A}$ with the rank of the augmented matrix. The rank counts the genuinely independent equations (@sec-gauss-jordan-rank explains it fully). If adding $\vect{b}$ increases the rank, $\vect{b}$ brings in an equation that contradicts the others, and there is no solution:

```matlab
A2 = [1 1 1; 1 -1 1; 2 0 2];
b2 = [3; 1; 5];
[rank(A2), rank([A2 b2])]
```

```{.text .code-output}
ans =

     2     3
```
:::

The ranks are 2 and 3, so the system of Example 2 has no solution. With $b_3 = 4$ instead, as in Example 3, both ranks would be 2, and there would be infinitely many solutions.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A system of linear equations has the solutions $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 0)$. What else can you say?

It has infinitely many solutions: every point on the line through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 0)$, which is $x + y = 3$, is a solution.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Can a homogeneous system be inconsistent?

No. $\vect{x} = \zerovec$ always solves $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## In the column picture, why does $\det\M{A} = 0$ for a $2 \times 2$ matrix mean that most right-hand sides can't be reached?

$\det\M{A} = 0$ means the two columns lie along the same line through the origin, so every combination of them lies on that line too. Only vectors $\vect{b}$ on that line can be made.
:::

## Key ideas

- A system of linear equations can be written as $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$, or as an augmented matrix $[\M{A} \mid \vect{b}]$.
- In the row picture, each equation is a line or plane, and a solution is a point on all of them.
- In the column picture, the system asks how much of each column of $\M{A}$ to take to make $\vect{b}$. Reading down gives the columns; reading across gives the equations back.
- Every system has exactly one solution, none or infinitely many: two solutions always give a whole line of them.
- A square system has exactly one solution for every $\vect{b}$ when $\det\M{A} \neq 0$.
- Every solution of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ is one particular solution plus a solution of the homogeneous system $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$.

## Exercises {#sec-linear-systems-exercises}

1. []{#exercise-linear-systems-1}Write this system as $\M{A}\vect{x} = \vect{b}$ and as an augmented matrix:
   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   3x_1 - 2x_3 &= 4 \\
   x_1 + x_2 + x_3 &= 0 \\
   2x_2 - x_3 &= 5
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   [Solution to exercise 1](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-1){.sol-link}

2. []{#exercise-linear-systems-2}Sketch the row picture of each system, and say whether it has one solution, none or infinitely many. Find the solution where there is exactly one.

   (a) $x + 2y = 4$ and $3x - y = 5$
   (b) $2x - 4y = 6$ and $-x + 2y = -3$
   (c) $x - y = 1$ and $2x - 2y = 5$

   [Solution to exercise 2](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-2){.sol-link}

3. []{#exercise-linear-systems-3}Write the system in Exercise 2(a) in the column picture, and check your solution by combining the columns.

   [Solution to exercise 3](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-3){.sol-link}

4. []{#exercise-linear-systems-4}For which values of $k$ and $c$ does the system $x + ky = 2$, $3x + 6y = c$ have (a) exactly one solution, (b) no solution, (c) infinitely many solutions?

   [Solution to exercise 4](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-4){.sol-link}

5. []{#exercise-linear-systems-5}(a) Show that if $\vect{h}_1$ and $\vect{h}_2$ both solve $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$, then so does $s\vect{h}_1 + t\vect{h}_2$ for any numbers $s$ and $t$.
   (b) Show that if $\M{A}\vect{p} = \vect{b}$ and $\M{A}\vect{h} = \zerovec$, then $\M{A}(\vect{p} + \vect{h}) = \vect{b}$.
   (c) Show that if $\M{A}\vect{p} = \vect{b}$ and $\M{A}\vect{q} = \vect{b}$, then $\vect{q} - \vect{p}$ solves $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$. Explain why (b) and (c) together prove @eq-general-solution. (*Hint*: each part needs only $\M{A}(\vect{u} + \vect{v}) = \M{A}\vect{u} + \M{A}\vect{v}$ and $\M{A}(c\vect{u}) = c\M{A}\vect{u}$.)

   [Solution to exercise 5](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-5){.sol-link}

6. []{#exercise-linear-systems-6}Propane ($\mathrm{C_3H_8}$), the gas in camping stoves, burns to give carbon dioxide and water. Balance $a\,\mathrm{C_3H_8} + b\,\mathrm{O_2} \to c\,\mathrm{CO_2} + d\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ with the smallest whole numbers.

   [Solution to exercise 6](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-6){.sol-link}

[]{#exercise-linear-systems-7}Describe in words, or with a sketch, how three planes can be arranged so that the system has (a) exactly one solution, (b) infinitely many solutions forming a line, (c) infinitely many solutions forming a plane, (d) no solution, in as many different ways as you can.

   [Solution to exercise 7](../appendices/solutions-2.qmd#solution-linear-systems-7){.sol-link}

## In practice

- **Mass balances**: chemical engineers track each substance through a plant, with one equation per substance per unit: what goes in equals what comes out, plus what is made, minus what is used. A large plant gives thousands of equations.
- **Electrical circuits**: Kirchhoff's laws, that the currents into any junction add up to zero and the voltages around any closed loop add up to zero, give one linear equation per junction or loop. Circuit simulators solve them for every component (@sec-circuits).
- **Structures**: in a bridge or roof truss, the forces at every joint must balance, giving one equation per joint and direction (@sec-trusses).
- **Balancing chemical equations**, as in Example 4, and finding which reactions are possible in a network of them.
- **Data fitting**: fitting a straight line to many measured points gives far more equations than unknowns, solved in the least-squares sense (@sec-orthogonality-least-squares).

## Going further

- A system is called **ill-conditioned** when its lines or planes are *nearly* parallel. Then the crossing point moves a long way when the numbers change a little, and small measurement or rounding errors can ruin the answer. @sec-floating-point-conditioning shows how to measure this.
- The idea that solutions are "a particular solution plus anything that solves the homogeneous system" reappears for differential equations, where it is called the complementary function plus particular integral (@sec-linear-odes).
- The set of right-hand sides $\vect{b}$ that can be reached, and the set of solutions of $\M{A}\vect{x} = \zerovec$, are called the **column space** and the **null space** of $\M{A}$. They are the subject of @sec-fundamental-subspaces.
